prompt.context: A US health care provider (H Health) suffered a profit decline last year. H Health signs contracts with patients and provides medical services through 300 contracted physicians. The key revenues come from commissions. A referral is necessary when certain medical treatment or service cannot be provided by H Health's contracted physicians. You have been hired to solve this problem.
prompt.question: H Health has experienced a profit decline last year. How would you approach diagnosing and solving this problem?

clarifying_info.q: What are H Health's key revenue sources?
clarifying_info.a: The key revenues come from commissions.

clarifying_info.q: How does H Health deliver services?
clarifying_info.a: H Health signs contracts with patients and provides medical services through 300 contracted physicians.

clarifying_info.q: What is a referral in this context?
clarifying_info.a: A referral is required when certain medical treatment or service cannot be provided by H Health's contracted physicians.

exhibits.title: H Health vs. Sunshine Competitor Comparison
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of H Health and its competitor Sunshine across number of patients and referral cost per member per month.

framework: Revenue drivers: number of patients x unit price
Cost drivers: variable costs (visits, referrals) and fixed costs (physician salaries)
Hypothesize revenue decline: fewer patients, lower unit price, lost market share to competitors
Hypothesize cost increase: more visits (e.g. flu season), higher per-visit cost, higher referral cost, physician salary increases
Focus investigation on referral costs as a key lever given H Health's higher referral cost vs. competitor

questions.prompt: Question 1: How would you approach diagnosing the profit decline?
questions.guidance: Candidate should decompose profit into Revenue minus Cost. Revenue = number of patients x unit price. Cost = variable cost (including referrals and visits) + fixed cost (physician salaries). Strong candidates list multiple hypotheses for both revenue decline and cost increase, such as: Revenue: fewer patients, lower prices, competitive pressure. Cost: more visits per patient (e.g. flu), higher per-visit cost, higher referral cost, higher physician salaries.

questions.prompt: Question 2: Competitor analysis — why is H Health's referral cost higher than the competitor Sunshine?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm structural reasons: (1) Economies of scale — Sunshine has 500,000 patients vs H Health's 300,000, so fixed admin costs are spread over more members. (2) Lower administration costs. (3) More contracted physicians reducing need for external referrals. Candidate should recognize scale as the primary driver.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Assuming none of H Health's contracted physicians have the specialty of cardiology, estimate the number of referrals per year for cardiology. Use: 300,000 patients total; 20% are over 65 years old and 30% of them need cardiology treatment; for those under 65, there is a 10% chance they require treatment; each treatment requires 5 visits per year.
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment the population by age, apply the appropriate probability to each segment, sum the patients needing treatment, then multiply by visits per year.

math.setup: Segment into >65 and <65 groups, apply treatment probability, multiply by 5 visits/year.
steps: Over-65 patients needing treatment: 300,000 x 0.20 x 0.30 = 18,000
Under-65 patients needing treatment: 300,000 x 0.80 x 0.10 = 24,000
Total referral visits per year: 42,000 x 5 = 210,000

questions.prompt: Question 4: The actual number of referrals is 300,000, which is higher than the estimate of 210,000. Why might this be?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose several structural or behavioral reasons: H Health's patient mix skews older than the general population; the 5 visits per year assumption was an underestimate; some patients request referrals even without a true medical need; physicians over-refer because they are risk-averse or lack motivation to handle cases they could manage themselves.

questions.prompt: Question 5: How much does the number of referrals need to decrease to justify the following incentive plan? Incentive plan: $100,000/year bonus to top 10 physicians with the lowest referral rate; $1,000,000 one-time training cost. Referral cost is $200 per referral; current referrals are 300,000.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total incremental cost of the incentive plan, then divide by the saving per referral to find the break-even reduction in referral volume.

math.setup: Calculate total cost of incentive plan; divide by referral cost per referral to find break-even number of referrals to eliminate.
steps: Total incentive plan cost: $100,000 x 10 physicians + $1,000,000 training = $2,000,000
Break-even referral reduction: $2,000,000 / $200 per referral = 10,000 referrals
math.answer: Referrals must decrease by 10,000 to break even on the incentive plan

questions.prompt: Question 6: If the incentive plan reduces referrals by 5% in year one and 2% in year two, what is the total net saving over two years?
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply 5% reduction to year-one base, then 2% to the reduced year-two base, calculate gross savings from eliminated referrals at $200 each, then subtract total incentive plan costs of $2,000,000 per year.

math.setup: Year 1: 5% reduction from 300,000. Year 2: 2% reduction from (300,000 - Y1 reduction). Gross savings = total referrals eliminated x $200. Net savings = gross savings - (2 x $2,000,000).
steps: Total incentive plan cost over 2 years: $2,000,000 x 2 = $4,000,000
math.answer: Total net saving over two years is $140,000

questions.prompt: Question 7: Apart from cardiology, how can H Health reduce referrals in general?
questions.guidance: Candidate should generate multiple levers across physician capability, incentives, patient relationships, and network: increase physician training to expand specialty coverage; extend the incentive program to other specialties and departments; improve physician-patient relationships to build trust and reduce unnecessary referrals; identify and address outlier physicians with disproportionately high referral rates; increase the total number of contracted physicians; partner with other providers to lower per-referral costs.

brainstorming.prompt: Apart from cardiology, how can H Health reduce the number of referrals across all specialties?

categories.name: Physician capability
ideas: Increase training to improve physicians' clinical capabilities
Hire or contract additional specialists to reduce gaps
Increase total number of contracted physicians

categories.name: Incentives and accountability
ideas: Extend the bonus incentive program to other departments
Identify and improve or remove physicians with outlier-high referral rates
Create transparency around individual physician referral rates

categories.name: Patient relationship and trust
ideas: Build patient trust so they accept in-network treatment
Educate patients on when referrals are medically necessary

categories.name: Network and cost management
ideas: Partner with other health care providers to lower referral cost per visit
Negotiate volume-based referral rate agreements with specialists

recommendation: H Health should prioritize reducing referral costs, which are higher than the competitor Sunshine ($20 vs $15 per member per month)
The most direct lever is reducing unnecessary referrals through a physician incentive and training program
The two-year incentive plan for cardiology alone yields only $140,000 in net savings, so the program must be expanded broadly to be material
risks: Physician morale and relationship risk if incentive/accountability measures are perceived as punitive
Patient dissatisfaction if referral restrictions prevent access to needed specialist care
Scale of savings may be insufficient — broad rollout and cost-per-referral reduction via partnerships are needed to meaningfully improve profitability
next_steps: Quantify referral volumes and costs across all specialties to size the full opportunity
Extend incentive and training program to all high-referral specialties
Explore partnerships with specialists to negotiate lower per-referral rates
Analyze patient mix to determine whether older/higher-risk population skew is addressable through targeted wellness or preventive programs
